title: Bereshit: you can rule over it (Genesis 4:7)
hookLine: God tells Cain the urge crouches, but he can master it

cards: You know the moment. Someone says something sharp, and a reply rises in your throat, already loaded. The phone is face-down on the table and your hand is already reaching.
A terrible day, and the cabinet with the cookies right there. The pull feels like it's already decided. Cain knew that moment.
His offering wasn't accepted and his brother's was, his face fell, and something hot rose in him. And right then, before anything happened, God spoke to him.

teach.b: Here's the verse: "If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it."
Sin crouches at the door, like an animal waiting. It wants you. But you can rule over it.

It's the first time the word sin appears in the Torah, and it arrives with a promise: you're not helpless. The rabbis gave that crouching thing a name: yetzer hara, the evil inclination, or better, the selfish urge.

teach.h: YETZER: FROM THE ROOT TO FORM.
teach.b: Yetzer comes from a root meaning to form, the same root used when God formed the first human from the dust. The urge is part of how people are made. And here's the surprise: the rabbis don't call it simply bad.

teach.h: WITHOUT IT, NO ONE BUILDS A HOUSE.
teach.b: The midrash says that without it, no one would build a house, marry, have children or start a business.

teach.h: WHO IS MIGHTY? WHO RULES THE URGE.
teach.b: That's why, it says, God looked at creation and called it very good, urge and all. The urge is energy; the question is who's steering.
The Talmud has God say: I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its remedy. And Pirkei Avot asks: who is mighty? The one who conquers their own urge, not the one who never feels it.
Cain, the story goes on, didn't rule it. He went out to the field with his brother. But the verse was spoken before that, and it stayed in the Torah for everyone after him.
The urge crouches. It isn't the one in charge. You can rule it.

how: Jewish ethical teaching speaks of the yetzer hara and the yetzer hatov, the selfish and the good inclinations, and treats study, prayer and habit as ways to steer the urge rather than erase it.

games.q: you're Cain. your offering was passed over and your brother's accepted. your face has fallen. what does God tell you?
o: sin crouches at the door, but you can rule over it.
games.why: "thou mayest rule over it." the warning comes before anything happens. the tragedy is that Cain didn't.

practice: Sit still, and within a minute some urge will show up: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, check the time, open your eyes. Don't fight it and don't follow it; just notice it crouching at the door, and name it: there's the urge.
Breathe once more before you do anything, because that breath is ruling it.

wordCard.voice: Yetzer hara. The selfish urge: part of how we're formed, full of energy, crouching at the door, and something a person can rule.

orig.note: Hebrew: the evil or selfish inclination; yetzer is from a root meaning to form.

carryVoice: Your line: you can rule it. The urge is energy, and you do the steering. Day one hundred sixty-four in the books.
